title: Florida Power & Light Co. v. Westinghouse Electric Corp.
lead: A nuclear-project disposal promise assumed reprocessing would remain available, but governmental changes and licensing barriers left only temporary onsite storage and uncertain future alternatives.

actors.name: Florida Power & Light
actors.role: Utility seeking spent-fuel removal and storage costs

proceedings: First district ruling rejected excuse; second allocated ultimate costs to the utility; third placed permanent storage costs on Westinghouse.
Fourth Circuit reversed future-storage liability and affirmed the unappealed reracking allocation.
limits: This disposal appeal was distinct from settled fixed-price uranium litigation. Nuclear policy and facilities are described as of the historical decision. The court confined its holding to impossibility/impracticability and did not change unappealed interim costs.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: The utility selects nuclear generation at Turkey Point
sections.cue: The disposal option requires removal from the site
paragraphs: Florida Power & Light sought a less costly alternative to transporting coal or oil and selected Westinghouse’s pressurized-water reactor after comparing proposals. Extended negotiations produced a 1966 contract for construction, fixed-price uranium for the first ten operating years, and disposal options for fuel generated during that period. The project expanded to two plants, reaching initial criticality in October 1972 and June 1973.

Florida elected Option C informally in 1970 and formally in 1972: Westinghouse would remove irradiated fuel and dispose of it as it chose. That promised offsite removal, not indefinite retention at the plant. The agreement developed against federal promotion of peaceful nuclear power and reprocessing that recovered valuable uranium and plutonium. In 1957 the Atomic Energy Commission assured utilities of government reprocessing if reasonable private service was unavailable. Government facilities processed private fuel, and commercial operations also existed before this contract.

sections.title: The expected route disappears
sections.cue: Attempts to secure Barnwell do not produce an executed agreement
paragraphs: Beginning in 1969, Westinghouse negotiated with Allied General Nuclear Services for the proposed Barnwell facility. An April 1970 letter of intent depended on a mutually acceptable agreement. A 1974 draft remained unsigned because regulatory changes increased anticipated costs and uncertainty. When Florida requested removal in 1975, Westinghouse cited the facility’s uncertain future. Florida was already reracking fuel onsite and sued for performance or damages.

Environmental proceedings, licensing obstacles, policy shifts, and President Carter’s indefinite commercial-reprocessing deferral deprived the industry of that route. Reracking was temporary. President Reagan’s later lifting of the ban and the Nuclear Waste Policy Act of 1982 did not supply a licensed reprocessor or available offsite repository when performance was due; future federal storage remained delayed and contingent at this appeal.

sections.title: Three district rulings allocate the consequences differently
sections.cue: The final judgment puts future permanent storage on Westinghouse
paragraphs: The district court’s June 25, 1981 opinion rejected excuse but deferred remedy, viewing reprocessing as speculative, risk as assumed, and Westinghouse’s diligence as deficient. It analogized to Suez Canal cases with a reasonably available alternative shipping route and encouraged equitable resolution.

After additional evidence, experts, and the 1982 legislation, an unreported second opinion found performance vitally different from reasonable expectations. It charged Westinghouse reracking but left remaining interim and ultimate costs with Florida, anticipating rate recovery. On Florida’s rehearing request, the November 8, 1984 third opinion restored much of the original rejection of excuse, divided reracking, and charged Westinghouse future permanent storage. That third judgment was on appeal.

sections.title: The appellate court identifies the basic assumption and unexpected event
sections.cue: The obstacle is not merely an unfavorable price change
paragraphs: Judge Donald Russell, joined by Widener and Butzner, confined decision to impossibility or commercial impracticability despite other pleaded defenses. Under Opera Company, an unexpected occurrence whose nonoccurrence was a basic assumption had to make performance impracticable. The equitable inquiry could apply even to an unqualified promise, considering assumed means, reasonable substitutes, risk, and responsibility for the obstacle.

No permanent offsite alternative existed at formation. Negotiations, documents, contract references, and the fuel-cycle price assumed reprocessing costs and recovered-material value. Florida also bore disposal for later plant years and therefore shared a stake in feasibility. Gardner’s contemporary memorandum worried about future plutonium prices, not whether demonstrated reprocessing technology worked. That differed from Wegematic’s unproved technological promise.

Even if private reprocessing disappointed, government assurances supplied a fallback. Their abandonment, rather than recovered-material price fluctuation, was the unforeseen contingency. The district court had already invoked that failed commitment to excuse timing in interim-cost analysis; the appellate court found it inconsistent to ignore it for the disposal obligation.

sections.title: No reasonable alternative or avoidable failure is established
sections.cue: The disposal undertaking is fundamentally transformed
paragraphs: Converting Barnwell to storage needed licensing, and its owner was uninterested. The district court itself would not find Westinghouse could force conversion or construct a viable facility. Similar political and licensing barriers defeated governmental and commercial efforts; the record did not show greater zeal would overcome them. Westinghouse repeatedly sought agreement while the proposed processor delayed over regulatory uncertainty.

Future federal storage was unlike sailing around the Cape after Suez closure: unavailable when due and still uncertain. An anticipated reprocessing gain of $18–20 million would become a loss over $80 million. Comparing that change to the entire plant project’s revenues obscured the separate disposal undertaking. Hadley also supported rejecting damages different in kind from contemplated reprocessing price risks: compulsory costly storage in an unavailable repository after abandoned government reprocessing.

The court additionally regarded it equitable for the beneficiaries of substantial nuclear-generation savings to bear unforeseen costs, consistent with congressional policy and later-year disposal treatment. It anticipated possible utility rate recovery without setting rates or entering judgment against consumers.

sections.title: Future-storage liability is reversed
paragraphs: On August 12, 1987, the Fourth Circuit held Westinghouse’s disposal duty excused by impossibility or commercial impracticability and reversed liability for future federal storage of the first ten years’ spent fuel. It affirmed the existing reracking allocation because neither party appealed it. The formal result was affirmance in part and reversal in part, without eliminating that interim obligation or deciding the separate earlier uranium-supply controversy.
